We have a task: identify the organic compound from experimental data. We have mass spec: m/z 193.1103 (intensity 100) etc. That suggests molecular weight ~193.11. The isotopic pattern shows M+1 at 194.1135 (12.5% relative). That is typical for a molecule with one nitrogen (N adds 1.1%? Actually N-14 vs N-15 0.37%? Not that). But C13 adds ~1.1% per carbon. For 11 carbons, M+1 ~11% from C13 plus maybe N? So 12.5% matches C11. So formula likely C11H15NO2 (as we derived). DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1 = 11 - 15/2 + 1/2 +1 = 11 -7.5 +0.5 +1 =5. So DBE=5. That could be aromatic ring (4 DBE) + carbonyl (1) =5. So likely a phenyl ring plus carbonyl and maybe hetero atoms.

Carbon NMR peaks: 166.40 (likely carbonyl C=O), 144.78, 132.00, 130.07 (x2), 127.80 (x2) aromatic carbons, 52.24 (maybe O-CH2), 49.55, 43.55, 19.23 (alkyl). So aromatic ring present.

Proton NMR not yet measured. Could get but maybe not needed.

We have candidate isomers from isomer list. Need to match NMR data.

Our carbon NMR experimental: 166.40 (C=O), aromatic carbons around 144-127, plus aliphatic: 52.24 (likely O-CH2), 49.55, 43.55, 19.23.

Let's examine candidate SMILES that match formula C11H15NO2.

List includes:

1. 'CCOC1=C(C=CC=N1)C(=O)C(C)C' (ethyl ester? Actually O-ethyl attached to pyridine? Contains N in aromatic ring, carbonyl attached to isopropyl? Let's compute carbon types: carbonyl 166, aromatic N heterocycle maybe shift 144, etc. O-CH2 (52). Additional aliphatic: isopropyl (CH, CH3). 19.23 could be methyl. 49.55 maybe CH attached to carbonyl? 43.55 maybe CH2 next to N? Not sure.

2. 'CC1(CC2=C(CCC(=O)N2)C(=O)C1)C' (some bicyclic). Might have two carbonyls (two 166). But we only see one carbonyl peak. So not.

3. 'CC1=C(C=CC=C1O)C2COCCN2' (phenoxy with morpholine). Contains O-CH2 (52), N-CH2 (maybe 49), etc. But has phenol OH (maybe shift 166? No carbonyl). So not.

4. 'CN(C)[C@H]1[C@H](COC2=CC=CC=C12)O' (dimethylamino, cyclic). Contains carbonyl? No. So not.

5. 'CN(C)CCC1=C2C(=CC=C1)OCO2' (no carbonyl). Not.

6. 'CCC[C@@](C1=CC=CC=C1)(C(=O)N)O' (tert-butyl? Actually a benzylic carbon attached to carbonyl amide and OH). Contains carbonyl (amide) 166, aromatic, O-CH (maybe 52). But also OH. Might match.

7. 'CC(=C[C@H]1[C@@H](C1(C)C)C(=O)OC)C#N' (nitrile, carbonyl, etc). Contains nitrile (no N in formula? nitrile adds N). But formula C11H15NO2? nitrile adds N, carbonyl O2, okay. But aromatic? No aromatic. Our carbon NMR shows many aromatic carbons, so not.

8. 'CC1=C2CCCCC2=C(N1C)C(=O)O' (indole? Actually quinoline? Contains aromatic heterocycle, carbonyl carboxylic acid). Might have aromatic carbons many. But OCH2? Not.

9. 'COC(=O)CC1=CC=CC(=C1)CCN' (ethyl ester of phenylpropyl amine). Contains carbonyl (ester) 166, aromatic, OCH2 (52), CH2 next to N (49), CH2 next to carbonyl (43?), CH3 (19). This seems plausible.

10. 'COC1=CC=CC2=C1CCN2CCO' (benzodioxole? Actually methoxy phenyl fused with ethoxy? Contains OCH3 (maybe 52?), OCH2CH2N etc. No carbonyl. Not.

11. 'CC(C1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)CCN)O' (tert-butyl phenyl with carbonyl and amine). Contains carbonyl, aromatic, OCH (maybe 52), CH3 (19). Could match.

12. 'C1C(OC(O1)C2=CC=CC=C2)CCN' (some cyclic ether). No carbonyl.

13. 'CC1(CCN(C1)C2=CC=CC=C2O)O' (phenol, tertiary amine). No carbonyl.

14. 'CCC1=C(C=CC2=C1C(CCO2)N)O' (some heterocycle). Contains carbonyl? No.

15. 'COC1=CC=C2CCC/C(=N\\O)/C2C1' (oxime). Contains carbonyl? Not.

16. 'C[C@@H]1C=C1C2C(C2NC(=O)C(=O)C)C' (multiple carbonyls). Not.

17. 'C1CC1N2CCC(C2)(C3=COC=C3)O' (no carbonyl).

18. 'CCOC(=O)C(C)C1=C(N=CC=C1)C' (ethyl ester attached to aromatic heterocycle). Contains carbonyl, aromatic N, OCH2 (52). Might match.

19. 'C1=CC(=CC=C1CCC(=O)O)CCN' (phenylpropionic acid with amine). Contains carbonyl (carboxylic acid) 166, aromatic, CH2CH2 (49,43), maybe OCH2? Not.

20. 'CNC1(CC1)C2=C(C(=CC=C2)OC)O' (phenol, tertiary amine). No carbonyl.

We need to match carbon NMR peaks: 166.40 (carbonyl). Aromatic peaks: 144.78 (likely aromatic carbon attached to hetero or carbonyl), 132.00, 130.07 (two), 127.80 (two). That's 6 aromatic carbons. Aromatic ring has 6 carbons, but we have 6 distinct peaks (some duplicates). So likely a monosubstituted phenyl (para? Actually monosubstituted phenyl gives 4 distinct aromatic carbons (two pairs). But we have 6 distinct, maybe a disubstituted aromatic with different substituents causing each carbon unique. Could be a phenyl with two substituents (e.g., para-substituted gives 4 distinct). But we have 6 distinct, maybe a heteroaromatic (pyridine) where each carbon distinct.

The aromatic peaks include a high 144.78 (likely C attached to hetero N or O). The others around 130-127 typical for phenyl.

Thus candidate with pyridine ring (hetero aromatic) may have distinct carbons.

Option 1: 'CCOC1=C(C=CC=N1)C(=O)C(C)C' is ethoxy-pyridine carbonyl isopropyl. Aromatic pyridine has 5 carbons, each distinct, plus carbonyl carbon (166). That matches 6 aromatic peaks? Actually pyridine has 5 aromatic carbons, plus maybe carbonyl carbon is separate. But we have 6 aromatic peaks (including 144). So could be pyridine (5) + maybe one more aromatic carbon from something else? But we only have pyridine ring (5). The carbonyl carbon is 166, not aromatic. So we need 5 aromatic peaks, but we have 6. However we have 6 peaks: 144.78, 132.00, 130.07 (x2), 127.80 (x2). That's 6 peaks, but two are duplicates (two at 130.07, two at 127.80). So distinct peaks: 144.78, 132.00, 130.07, 127.80 = 4 distinct. So maybe duplicates due to symmetry. So 4 distinct aromatic carbons, consistent with monosubstituted phenyl (para? Actually monosubstituted phenyl gives 4 distinct: ipso, ortho (2 same), meta (2 same), para). So 4 distinct peaks matches.

Thus aromatic is phenyl, not pyridine.

Thus candidate with phenyl ring.

Which candidates have phenyl ring and carbonyl? Options 9, 11, 18, 19.

Let's examine each.

Option 9: 'COC(=O)CC1=CC=CC(=C1)CCN' This is methyl ester of phenylpropyl amine? Actually structure: methyl ester of 4-(2-aminopropyl)benzoic acid? Wait: COC(=O) is methyl ester attached to CH2-CH2- phenyl? Actually COC(=O)CC1=... So carbonyl attached to CH2CH2- phenyl. So carbonyl carbon (ester) 166, OCH3 (52?), CH2 next to carbonyl (43), CH2 next to phenyl (49), aromatic 6 carbons (4 distinct). Also there is amine on side chain (CH2CH2N). No extra OCH2. The OCH3 is 52? Actually OCH3 shift ~52? In carbon NMR, OCH3 appears around 52 ppm. Good. So we have OCH3 (52.24) matches. Then CH2 next to carbonyl (C=O-CH2) appears ~43.55 (makes sense). CH2 next to phenyl (CH2-Ph) appears ~49.55 (maybe). Methyl of isopropyl? Not present. We have 19.23 (maybe CH3 of something). But we have no CH3 besides OCH3. Wait OCH3 is 52, not 19. So 19.23 could be a methyl attached to aromatic? Not present. So maybe not.

Option 11: 'CC(C1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)CCN)O' This is a tertiary alcohol attached to phenyl carbonyl side chain? Actually structure: isopropanol attached to phenyl carbonyl? Let's parse: CC(C1=... )O is a secondary alcohol (isopropyl) attached to phenyl carbonyl side chain? The SMILES: CC(C1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)CCN)O. So there is a phenyl attached to carbonyl (C=O) attached to CH2CH2N (propyl amine). Also there is a tertiary alcohol (C(CH3)(OH)- attached to phenyl? Actually the phenyl is attached to the carbon bearing OH and CH3? The central carbon is attached to CH3, OH, and phenyl carbonyl side chain. So there is a CH3 (19.23), a carbon bearing OH (maybe 52?), but carbon bearing OH (C attached to O) appears ~70 ppm, not 52. But we have 52.24 maybe OCH3 not OH. So maybe not.

Option 18: 'CCOC(=O)C(C)C1=C(N=CC=C1)C' This is ethyl ester attached to a pyridine ring (hetero aromatic). Not phenyl.

Option 19: 'C1=CC(=CC=C1CCC(=O)O)CCN' This is phenyl with propionic acid (carboxylic acid) and ethylamine side chain? Actually phenyl-CH2-CH2-NH? Wait: phenyl-CH2-CH2-N? The SMILES: C1=CC(=CC=C1CCC(=O)O)CCN. So phenyl attached to propionic acid (COOH) and also attached to ethylamine (CH2CH2N). So there is a carboxylic acid carbonyl (166), aromatic, CH2CH2N (49,43), plus maybe no OCH3. No methyl at 19.23. So not.

Thus option 9 seems best: OCH3 (52), CH2CH2 (49,43), aromatic, carbonyl, plus maybe a methyl at 19.23? But we have no methyl. However there is a methyl group on the ester (OCH3) which appears at 52, not 19. So 19.23 could be a methyl attached to aromatic? Not present. Could be a methyl on the side chain? Not.

But maybe the 19.23 is the methyl of the ethyl group? Wait we have OCH3 (52) and maybe CH3 of ethyl attached to carbonyl? Actually the carbonyl is part of methyl ester: COC(=O)-. The methyl is OCH3 (52). The carbonyl carbon is 166. The carbonyl carbon attached to CH2 (CH2-COOCH3). The CH2 next to carbonyl is 43. The CH2 next to phenyl is 49. The phenyl has 6 carbons. No other methyl. So 19.23 maybe from impurity or maybe the CH3 of ethyl group? But there is no ethyl group besides OCH3. So maybe the 19.23 is from the methyl of the carbonyl? Wait OCH3 is attached to carbonyl, but carbon of OCH3 is sp3 attached to O, appears ~52. The methyl of ethyl (CH3-CH2-O) would be at ~14 ppm. Not 19. So maybe the 19.23 is from a methyl attached to aromatic (like tolyl). Not present.

Thus maybe the correct structure is 'CCOC1=C(C=CC=N1)C(=O)C(C)C' (option 1). Let's examine its carbon NMR: carbonyl 166, aromatic carbons (pyridine) maybe 144, 132, 130, 127 etc. Aliphatic: OCH2 (52), isopropyl: CH (49?), CH3 (19), CH3 (19) maybe duplicates. But we have only one 19.23 peak, maybe overlapping. Also we have 43.55 maybe carbon attached to carbonyl (C attached to carbonyl and isopropyl). In isopropyl, the carbon attached to carbonyl is a quaternary carbon? Actually structure: C(=O)C(C)C is isopropyl carbonyl (i.e., carbonyl attached to a carbon bearing two methyls). That carbon (tertiary) appears around 43-45 ppm. The two methyls appear around 19 ppm (maybe overlapping). So that matches 19.23 (maybe both overlapped). So option 1 fits well.

Also the formula C11H15NO2 matches. The pyridine ring has N, aromatic carbons distinct. Carbon NMR of pyridine ring would have a downfield carbon attached to N (~150). So 144.78 matches.

Thus option 1 seems best.

We can validate by simulating spectra earlier: we simulated for option 1 and got simulated carbon NMR: Deltas: 206.40, 160.30, 137.90, 130.27, 123.57, 122.45, 62.45, 37.30, 17.90, 17.90, 14.35. That does not match experimental (166 vs 206, etc). The simulated carbonyl at 206 is too high (maybe because it's a ketone vs ester?). Our experimental carbonyl at 166 suggests ester carbonyl. Option 1 has a ketone (C=O attached to isopropyl) not ester. So carbonyl shift 206 typical for ketone, not 166. So option 1 not match.

Option 9 simulated? Not yet. Let's simulate option 9.
